title: How do you model a composite primary key in JPA, and what is the difference between @EmbeddedId and @IdClass?
topicTitle: How do you model a composite primary key in JPA

s1_definition.profdef: A composite primary key is a key made of two or more columns together. JPA offers two ways to map it. `@EmbeddedId` uses a single embeddable key class annotated `@Embeddable`, and the entity holds one field of that type annotated `@EmbeddedId`; you access the parts through the key object, for example `statement.getId().getAccountId()`. `@IdClass` keeps the key fields as SEPARATE fields on the entity, each marked `@Id`, and you additionally declare a plain non-entity key class (listed in `@IdClass(...)`) whose field names and types mirror those id fields; the key class exists only so `findById` and the persistence context have a single object to represent the identity. Both require the key class to be `Serializable` and to implement `equals` and `hashCode`. `@EmbeddedId` is more object-oriented and groups the key cleanly; `@IdClass` reads more like plain columns and makes JPQL slightly simpler.
s1_definition.analogy: A monthly account statement at National Bank of India is uniquely identified by the account number PLUS the statement period, together. With `@EmbeddedId` you put those two values inside one little "key envelope" object and the statement carries that envelope. With `@IdClass` you keep the account number and period as two loose fields on the statement and separately describe a matching "key form" so the bank's filing system has one handle for the pair.
s1_definition.oneliner: `@EmbeddedId` embeds one `@Embeddable` key object (access via `getId().getX()`); `@IdClass` keeps separate `@Id` fields on the entity plus a mirror key class — both need `Serializable`, `equals`, and `hashCode`.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A composite primary key is a key made of two or more columns together. JPA offers two ways to map it. `@EmbeddedId` uses a single embeddable key class annotated `@Embeddable`, and the entity holds one field of that type annotated `@EmbeddedId`; you access the parts through the key object, for example `statement.getId().getAccountId()`. `@IdClass` keeps the key fields as SEPARATE fields on the entity, each marked `@Id`, and you additionally declare a plain non-entity key class (listed in `@IdClass(...)`) whose field names and types mirror those id fields; the key class exists only so `findById` and the persistence context have a single object to represent the identity. Both require the key class to be `Serializable` and to implement `equals` and `hashCode`. `@EmbeddedId` is more object-oriented and groups the key cleanly; `@IdClass` reads more like plain columns and makes JPQL slightly simpler.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** A monthly account statement at National Bank of India is uniquely identified by the account number PLUS the statement period, together. With `@EmbeddedId` you put those two values inside one little "key envelope" object and the statement carries that envelope. With `@IdClass` you keep the account number and period as two loose fields on the statement and separately describe a matching "key form" so the bank's filing system has one handle for the pair.

**One line to remember:** `@EmbeddedId` embeds one `@Embeddable` key object (access via `getId().getX()`); `@IdClass` keeps separate `@Id` fields on the entity plus a mirror key class — both need `Serializable`, `equals`, and `hashCode`.

sections.s3_banking:
Let me describe the real situation at National Bank of India that forced a composite key.

Problem 1 — a single-column key could not identify a statement. We generate one statement per account per month. Neither the account id alone nor the period alone is unique — Rajesh has twelve statements a year, and October has statements for thousands of accounts. The natural identity is the pair (account id, period) together. This is exactly what a composite primary key models: two columns that are unique only in combination.

Problem 2 — lookups and the identity map kept misbehaving. An early attempt used a generated surrogate id but then had to add a unique constraint on (account id, period) and look statements up by that pair anyway, which meant the surrogate key added nothing. Modelling the real composite identity directly made `findById` natural and made the persistence-context identity map correct — provided the key class implements `equals` and `hashCode` over both fields.

Problem 3 — we needed clean reads for the statement list screen. The screen lists a customer's statements for a year, so queries filter by account id and order by period. With `@EmbeddedId` those queries navigate through the key object, which the team found perfectly readable once the pattern was clear.

Here is what the mini-project code will do. There is a `StatementId` class annotated `@Embeddable`, implementing `Serializable`, `equals`, and `hashCode` over `accountId` and `period`. There is a `MonthlyStatement` entity with an `@EmbeddedId StatementId id` plus a `closingBalance`. A `YearMonthConverter` (`AttributeConverter`) stores the period as a `VARCHAR` like `2026-10`. The `StatementRepository` exposes `findById(StatementId)` and a derived finder `findByIdAccountId(String accountId)` that navigates into the embedded key. The `StatementService`, annotated `@Transactional`, creates a statement for (account, period) and reads it back by the composite key. The demo shows that two statements for the same account in different months coexist, and that looking up by the exact pair returns the right one. A test verifies `equals`/`hashCode` on the key.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is generating Rajesh's November statement and then reading his October statement back.

Step 1: `generate("SAV2001", "2026-11", 1050000)` builds a `StatementId` from the account id and the parsed `YearMonth`. The key object is the real identity of the row.

Step 2: We construct a `MonthlyStatement` carrying that `@EmbeddedId` and a closing balance, then call `repo.save(statement)`. Hibernate issues `INSERT INTO monthly_statements (account_id, period, closing_balance, generated_at) VALUES ('SAV2001', '2026-11', 1050000, now())`. The `period` is written as the string `2026-11` because the `YearMonthConverter` turns the `YearMonth` into a `VARCHAR`.

Step 3: Because the primary key is the pair (account_id, period), this row coexists peacefully with Rajesh's August, September, and October statements — the pair is unique even though neither column is unique alone.

Step 4: `getOne("SAV2001", "2026-10")` builds a `StatementId` for that exact pair and calls `repo.findById(id)`. Hibernate runs `SELECT ... WHERE account_id = 'SAV2001' AND period = '2026-10'`. The persistence-context identity map uses the key's `equals` and `hashCode` to recognise the entity, which is why implementing them correctly is mandatory.

Step 5: The result maps to a `StatementView`, reading the key parts through `getId().getAccountId()` and `getId().getPeriod()`. The view is a plain record, safe to return as JSON.

```
2026-10-24 00:35:14 INFO  StatementService - Generated statement for composite key (SAV2001, 2026-11)
2026-10-24 00:35:14 FINE  StatementService - INSERT monthly_statements (account_id='SAV2001', period='2026-11')
2026-10-24 00:35:14 INFO  StatementService - findById(StatementId{SAV2001,2026-10}) → 1 row
2026-10-24 00:35:14 INFO  StatementService - closingBalance=1000000.00 for (SAV2001, 2026-10)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client: GET /api/v1/statements/SAV2001/2026-10
    │
    ▼
  StatementController.getOne("SAV2001","2026-10")
    │
    ▼
  StatementService (@Transactional readOnly)
    │ id = new StatementId("SAV2001", YearMonth.of(2026,10))
    │ repo.findById(id)
    ▼
  Hibernate — composite key lookup
    │ SQL: SELECT * FROM monthly_statements
    │      WHERE account_id='SAV2001' AND period='2026-10'
    ▼
  PostgreSQL ── PRIMARY KEY (account_id, period) ──→ 1 row
    │
    ▼
  Response: {"accountId":"SAV2001","period":"2026-10","closingBalance":1000000.00}

  ── @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass ──
  @EmbeddedId: one @Embeddable key field on entity   → access via getId().getX()
               JPQL: WHERE s.id.accountId = :acc
  @IdClass   : separate @Id fields on entity + mirror → access via getAccountId()
               JPQL: WHERE s.accountId = :acc AND s.period = :p

  ── BOTH REQUIRE ──
  Serializable + no-arg ctor + equals/hashCode over ALL key fields
```

  Composite key models identity that needs 2+ columns (account + period).

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — @EmbeddedId Composite Key (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Value Object: StatementId is an immutable identity value         │
  │  Converter: YearMonthConverter maps value type ↔ VARCHAR          │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: StatementId owns identity; MonthlyStatement owns state        │
  │  O: new key part = change the embeddable, not every query call    │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │ @Embeddable StatementId        │ 1    1 │ @Entity MonthlyStatement       │
  │  accountId : String            │◆──────▶│  @EmbeddedId id : StatementId  │
  │  period : YearMonth            │        │  closingBalance : BigDecimal   │
  │  equals()/hashCode()           │        │  getId().getAccountId()        │
  │  Serializable                  │        └───────────────────────────────┘
  └───────────────────────────────┘

  @IdClass alternative:
    @Entity @IdClass(StatementKey.class) MonthlyStatement { @Id accountId; @Id period; }
    class StatementKey implements Serializable { accountId; period; equals/hashCode }

  ── Call Chain (lookup) ──
  1. Controller.getOne("SAV2001","2026-10")
  2.   Service builds StatementId
  3.     repo.findById(id) → WHERE account_id=? AND period=?

  ⚠ Missing/incorrect equals-hashCode breaks the identity map (merge/cache failures).
  Rule: prefer @EmbeddedId; use @IdClass for simpler JPQL or legacy schemas.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A composite primary key is an identity made of two or more columns that are unique only in combination, and JPA gives me two ways to map it. With EmbeddedId I create one key class annotated Embeddable and the entity holds a single field of that type annotated EmbeddedId, so I access the parts through the key object. With IdClass I keep the key fields as separate fields on the entity, each annotated Id, and I declare a separate mirror class in the IdClass annotation whose field names and types match, so the persistence context has one object to represent the identity. Both styles require the key class to be Serializable, to have a no-arg constructor, and to implement equals and hashCode over all the key fields, because Hibernate uses those methods in its identity map.

In our statement service at National Bank of India, a monthly statement is identified by the account id and the period together, since one account has many monthly statements and one month has statements for many accounts. I modelled that with EmbeddedId: a StatementId embeddable holding the account id and the year-month, and the MonthlyStatement entity carrying it. I look a statement up by constructing the StatementId and passing it to findById, and derived finders navigate into the key, for example findByIdAccountId. I also register an attribute converter so the year-month stores as a clean string column.

I default to EmbeddedId because grouping the key into one immutable value object models the identity as a real concept and reduces mistakes, and I reach for IdClass only when I want the id fields to sit directly on the entity for simpler JPQL or to match a legacy schema. The senior caution I always raise is that a broken equals or hashCode on the key class silently breaks merging and caching, so I implement them over every key field, and I build composite keys from stable business values like an account id and a period that never change, which is exactly the property you want in a primary key.
